You Already Know How to Count in Japanese 🧵

Hokage titles, Yonko, and Sannin have been teaching you Japanese numbers all along

Every time you called Minato "the Yondaime" you said four. Every time someone referenced the Sannin you said three. Every time you talked about the Yonko era in One Piece you said four again.

Which one surprised you most? Drop it below 👇

三代目 (sandaime) means the third-generation holder of the Hokage title. 三 (san) = 3, 代 (dai) = generation or succession, 目 (me) = ordinal suffix that turns a number into nth. The Third Hokage, Hiruzen Sarutobi, holds this title.

三人 (sannin) literally means three people. 三 (san) = 3, 人 (nin) = person or people counter. The legendary Sannin - Jiraiya, Tsunade, and Orochimaru - are simply the three people at the apex of Konoha's shinobi.

四皇 (Yonko) means Four Emperors. 四 (yon) = 4, 皇 (ko) = emperor. The four most powerful pirates who dominate the New World. The number is literally encoded in the title - if you know yon equals 4, the faction name tells you exactly how many there are.
七代目 (nanadaime) means the seventh-generation Hokage. 七 (nana) = 7, 代目 (daime) = nth-generation holder of a title. Naruto Uzumaki is the Nanadaime Hokage, the seventh person to hold the title.
七つ (nanatsu) is the native Japanese reading of 7, from the older counting system (hitotsu, futatsu, mittsu...). 七 (shichi) is the Sino-Japanese reading.

Learning Japanese with Homura (Demon Slayer: Mugen Train Theme) 🧵

Tamashii, kienai, and the Japanese vocabulary for what survives after someone is gone

If you saw Demon Slayer: Mugen Train in theatres, you know exactly when Homura starts playing and what happens when it does. The end of one of the most devastating moments in recent anime history, and then LiSA's voice comes in. You were not ready.

Homura (炎) means flame or fire in Japanese. The single kanji 炎 is the elevated literary form of fire, distinct from the more common 火 (hi, ordinary fire/flame). 炎 specifically suggests intense, upward-burning flame with a sense of power and spiritual presence.
Homura is N3-N2 in places, with pockets of N4 vocabulary. Key words like tamashii (soul/spirit), kienai (won't disappear/undying), inochi (life), and tsuyoku (strongly) are N3-N4.
Homura (炎) is performed by LiSA (Risa Oribe). The title means flame - specifically the archaic, poetic reading of the kanji 炎 that evokes intense spiritual fire.
Tamashii (魂) means soul, spirit, or essence - the deepest inner core of a person that persists beyond their physical existence.

Kienai (消えない) means won't disappear, undying, unfading. It combines kieru (消える, to disappear, to go out - used for flames, lights, and presences) with the negative nai (ない). So kienai is the negative of a flame going out: a flame that won't die.

What Do Naruto's Jutsu Names Actually Mean? 🧵

Every technique you've been yelling has a literal translation

Millions of people spent years yelling "RASENGAN" and "CHIDORI" and "KAGE BUNSHIN NO JUTSU" without knowing what any of those words mean. That's not a problem - that's just how anime absorption works. The phonetics come first. The meaning catches up later.
Rasengan (螺旋丸) means Spiraling Sphere. 螺旋 (rasen) means spiral or helix - the character 螺 depicts a spiral shell, and 旋 means to rotate. 丸 (maru) means sphere or round object.

Chidori (千鳥) means One Thousand Birds. Kakashi named the technique after the crackling sound the electrical current makes as it flows through the arm, which sounded to him like a flock of a thousand birds crying out at once.

Sharingan (写輪眼) means Copy Wheel Eye. 写 (sha) is the character for copy or imitate - the same one used in 写真 (shashin, photograph, literally copying truth). 輪 (rin) means wheel or ring, referring to the spinning tomoe pattern.

The Edo in Edo Tensei (穢土転生) uses completely different kanji from the historical city of Edo (江戸). Edo Tensei uses 穢土, meaning defiled earth or impure land - a Buddhist concept for the world of suffering as opposed to the Pure Land of paradise.

Rinnegan (輪廻眼) means Samsara Eye. 輪廻 (rinne) is the Japanese Buddhist term for samsara - the endless cycle of death, rebirth, and suffering. The same concept appears in 輪廻転生 (rinne tensei), the full phrase for reincarnation. 眼 (gan) means eye.

Guren no Yumiya Is the Hardest Japanese in Any Anime Opening 🧵

Every verse of Attack on Titan's iconic song translated and explained

You know the feeling. Guren no Yumiya drops, the drum beat hits, and suddenly you're convinced you could single-handedly join the Survey Corps.

Save this for your next rewatch 📸

Guren no Yumiya (紅蓮の弓矢) means Crimson Bow and Arrow. Guren (紅蓮) literally means crimson lotus, a Buddhist term for fierce red originating in the imagery of the eight cold hells where skin cracks open like red lotus petals.

It is one of the most linguistically dense anime openings ever written. The lyrics use N1-N2 classical vocabulary, furigana double-readings where the written kanji differs from the sung word, archaic verb forms like ずに and 死せる, and German interjections.
Wir sind der Jager is German for We are the hunter. It appears in the chorus and connects directly to Eren Jager's surname, which is the German word for hunter.
Guren no Yumiya is performed by Linked Horizon, a project by the composer and performer Revo, who is also the creative force behind Sound Horizon.
Linked Horizon writes one kanji compound as the visual meaning on the lyrics sheet, then shows a different simpler word in furigana as what the singer actually sings.

Learning Japanese with Silhouette (Naruto Shippuden Opening) 🧵

Oikakeru, kage, and how te iku encodes the direction that Sasuke is always going

Naruto Shippuden had sixteen openings by the time Silhouette arrived. By that point in the series, every fan knew exactly what Naruto was running toward and why he would never stop.

Which one surprised you most? Drop it below 👇

Silhouette is written in katakana as シルエット (shirueetto) in Japanese, where it is used with the same meaning as in English: the dark outline or shadow-shape of a figure seen against a lighter background.
Silhouette sits at N4 overall, making it accessible to intermediate beginners. Core vocabulary like kage (shadow), oikakeru (to chase after), and hashiru (to run) is N4-N3.

Silhouette is performed by KANA-BOON, a Japanese rock band from Osaka formed in 2008. The band consists of Maguro Taniguchi (vocals, guitar), Ryusei Kiuchi (guitar), Hiroyuki Motoyama (bass), and Yoshiya Okamoto (drums).

Oikakeru (追いかける) means to chase after, to pursue, to run after someone or something. It is a compound verb: oi (追い, the combining form of 追う, to chase) + kakeru (駆ける, to run, to race). Together: to run in pursuit of someone.

Kage (影) means shadow, silhouette, or the dark shape cast by something. In Japanese the same word covers both a shadow on the ground and the silhouette of a figure. It is also used metaphorically for a trace or vestige of something that was there.

Why Are Uchiha Jutsus Named After Japanese Gods? 🧵

The Shinto myths hiding inside Naruto's eye powers

When Itachi activates Tsukuyomi from his right eye, that is not a coincidence. When Amaterasu erupts from the left, that is not decoration.

Save this for your next rewatch 📸

Amaterasu (天照) is the Shinto goddess of the sun and ruler of the heavens, one of the most important deities in the Kojiki (712 CE). In the original myth, she was born when the god Izanagi washed his left eye after escaping the underworld.
That is exactly how the original myth works. In the Kojiki, when Izanagi washed his left eye, the sun goddess Amaterasu was born. When he washed his right eye, the moon god Tsukuyomi was born.

The Kojiki (古事記, Record of Ancient Matters) is Japan's oldest chronicle, compiled in 712 CE under Emperor Genmei. It records the creation myth, the age of the gods, and the genealogy of the imperial family.
Susanoo (スサノオ) is the Shinto god of storms, born when Izanagi washed his nose during the same purification ritual that produced Amaterasu and Tsukuyomi.
Izanagi (イザナギ) is the male creator deity of Japanese mythology who helped create the islands of Japan with his wife Izanami.

Bushido: The Samurai Code Running Every Anime You Watch 🧵

武士道 explained - the seven virtues behind Tanjiro's compassion, Zoro's loyalty, and Byakuya's honor

You know that moment when Tanjiro bows to a demon he just killed? When Zoro offers his life to Mihawk without hesitation? When Byakuya executes judgment on someone he loves because duty demands it?

Save this for your next rewatch 📸
Bushido (武士道, literally 'way of the warrior') is the code of moral conduct followed by the Japanese samurai class.

The seven virtues of Bushido are: Gi (義, righteousness/justice), Yu (勇, courage/bravery), Jin (仁, benevolence/compassion), Rei (礼, respect/etiquette), Makoto (誠, honesty/sincerity), Meiyo (名誉, honor/glory), and Chugi (忠義, loyalty/devotion).

The Hagakure (葉隠), written by samurai Yamamoto Tsunetomo around 1716, contains the most famous quote in samurai philosophy: Bushido to wa shinu koto to mitsuketari (武士道とは死ぬことと見つけたり), meaning 'The way of the samurai is found in death.
Tanjiro Kamado from Demon Slayer embodies the Bushido virtue of Jin (仁, benevolence/compassion), showing mercy even toward the demons he kills.

Zoro's entire character is built on Bushido's virtue of Chugi (忠義, loyalty). His absolute loyalty to Luffy, his oath to become the world's greatest swordsman, and his willingness to die for his captain are all classic Bushido values.

Learning Japanese with Blue Bird (Naruto Shippuden Opening) 🧵

Mama, todoku, and the precise vocabulary for chasing someone who keeps getting further away

Naruto Shippuden had a lot of great openings. But Blue Bird - the third OP by Ikimono-gakari - sits in a different category for most people who grew up watching it.

Which of these words have you caught in anime? Reply 👇
Blue Bird in Japanese is 青い鳥 (aoi tori). Aoi (青い) means blue or green-blue, a colour that in Japanese traditionally spans sky-blue through spring-green. Tori (鳥) means bird.
Blue Bird is N4 overall - accessible to learners at the beginner-to-intermediate transition. Core vocabulary like jiyuu (freedom), sora (sky), tori (bird), and koe (voice) is N5-N4.
Blue Bird is performed by Ikimonogakari (いきものがかり), a Japanese pop rock band formed in Kanagawa in 1999. The band's name roughly translates to The Animal Keeper or caretaker of living things.

Jiyuu no tori ni nareru (自由の鳥になれる) means I can become a bird of freedom. Jiyuu (自由) means freedom or liberty. No connects it as a modifier to tori (bird). Ni nareru is the potential form of ni naru (to become something) - can become.
Mama (まま) in Japanese grammar means in the unchanged state of / while remaining as. It attaches to a verb (past ta-form) or adjective to express staying in a condition without change.

Learning Japanese with We Are! (One Piece Opening) 🧵

Nakama, jiyuu, and why this is one of the best N5 listening exercises in anime

If you watched One Piece growing up - or even just caught the opening somewhere - you heard We Are! long before you ever thought about studying Japanese.

Which one surprised you most? Drop it below 👇

We Are is an English phrase used as the title of One Piece's first opening. In Japanese the lyrics mix English and Japanese freely. The English We Are functions as a declaration of crew identity - these people are a unit, a crew, a we.

We Are is N4-N5 level overall - one of the most beginner-friendly anime openings from a major series. Core vocabulary (yume for dream, tomodachi/nakama for friend/crewmate, susumu for advance, umi for sea) is N5-N4.

We Are is performed by Hiroshi Kitadani, a Japanese rock vocalist best known as a member of the band ZARD. He recorded We Are in 1999 for the first episode of One Piece and the song remained the opening through episode 47.

Nakama (仲間) is one of the most important words in One Piece and one of the most discussed in anime fandom. It means companion, crewmate, fellow, or person on the same team - but with an emotional weight that varies by context.

Susume (進め) is the bare imperative form of susumu (進む, to advance, to move forward, to make progress). The bare imperative in Japanese, without any politeness suffix, is a direct command. Susume means advance! or move forward! or keep going!

The samurai who lost everything when the Meiji era began

Save this for your next rewatch 📸
Rurouni Kenshin is set in Meiji 11, which is 1878. This is exactly one year after the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877 ended - the last major armed uprising of samurai against the Meiji government.

After 1868, samurai lost their hereditary stipends (abolished by 1876), were forbidden from carrying swords in public by the Haitōrei edict of 1876, and were reclassified as shizoku (warrior families) with no special privileges.
Saigo Takamori, the leader of the Satsuma Rebellion and widely called the last true samurai, is a key historical figure behind the manga's themes.

Saito Hajime was a real historical figure who served as a captain in the Shinsengumi, the elite pro-shogunate sword force. After the Meiji Restoration he reinvented himself as a police officer - exactly as depicted in Rurouni Kenshin. He lived until 1915.
The Haitōrei edict (廃刀令) was a law passed in March 1876 that prohibited anyone except military personnel and police officers from wearing swords in public.

Every Japanese Day of the Week Has an Anime Character in It 🧵

Suicune for Wednesday, Mokuton for Thursday, Light Yagami's secret moon name for Monday - the complete mnemonic map

If you have been memorizing Japanese weekdays as random vocabulary, stop. They are not random. Japanese days of the week are a 1,400-year-old cosmological system, and every single element in that system already has a famous anime character living in it.

The seven days in Japanese are: Nichiyobi (Sunday, 日曜日), Getsuyobi (Monday, 月曜日), Kayobi (Tuesday, 火曜日), Suiyobi (Wednesday, 水曜日), Mokuyobi (Thursday, 木曜日), Kinyobi (Friday, 金曜日), Doyobi (Saturday, 土曜日).

Japanese days of the week are based on the ancient Chinese system of the Seven Luminaries (七曜, shichiyou) - the Sun, Moon, and five classical planets visible to the naked eye (Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn).

Suicune's Japanese name is Suikun (スイクン). The first two syllables, sui (スイ), come from the Japanese word for water, 水 (sui/mizu). This is the same sui in 水曜日 (Suiyobi, Wednesday), which literally means the day of water.
Mokuton (木遁) uses the kanji 木 (moku/ki), meaning wood or tree. Thursday in Japanese is 木曜日 (Mokuyobi), which starts with the same 木 character read the same way: moku.
Light Yagami's Japanese name is written 夜神月 (Yagami Raito). The kanji for his first name is 月, which means moon.

How a 6th-century koi myth became Magikarp's design blueprint

The Dragon Gate legend (龍門, Ryūmon) is a well-documented Chinese and Japanese folk legend, originating in the Shuijing Zhu (6th century CE). It describes koi climbing a waterfall on the Yellow River and transforming into dragons upon reaching the top.
In the Japanese retelling, demons attracted to the koi's glittering scales would raise the height of the waterfall whenever a fish got close to the top.

Magikarp's Japanese name Koikingu (コイキング) directly references koi (鯉, carp). The mechanic - a long grind with a useless Pokémon that transforms into a powerful dragon - mirrors the koi no takinobori legend directly.

鯉の滝登り (koi no takinobori) means the climbing of the waterfall by the carp. It is a Japanese proverb for achieving something against overwhelming odds, composed of koi (carp), no (possessive particle), taki (waterfall), and nobori (climbing).
In traditional versions the transformed dragon is not given a specific name - it is described as a golden dragon ascending to the heavens.

Ichigo sounds exactly like the Japanese word for strawberry (苺, ichigo). Tite Kubo made this a deliberate pun - Ichigo's hair is orange like a strawberry, but his name kanji (一護) means the one who protects.

Itachi (鼬) means weasel. The name IS the word - if you looked up weasel in a Japanese dictionary you would find itachi. Weasels in Japanese folklore are associated with bad omens and death arriving without warning, which fits Itachi Uchiha perfectly.

Gurenge (紅蓮華) means Red Lotus Flower. The kanji compound is made of three characters: gu (紅, crimson or deep red), ren (蓮, lotus plant), and ge (華, flower, blossom).

Gurenge is intermediate difficulty - mostly N4 to N3. The core vocabulary (yume for dream, kibou for hope, tsuyoku for strongly) is N4. Grammar patterns like hodo (the more X, the more Y) and tame ni (for the sake of) are N4.

Strongly so. The lotus (蓮, hasu or ren in Japanese) is one of the most important symbols in Buddhism. It grows rooted in mud at the bottom of ponds but blooms above the water's surface, pure and beautiful.
Tsuyoku nare (強くなれ) means Become stronger or Be strong. Tsuyoku is the adverbial form of tsuyoi (strong, powerful). Nare is the bare imperative of naru (to become). Together: become strong.
Kibou (希望) means hope. The two kanji are ki (希, rare, scarce) and bou (望, wish, desire, gaze). The combination captures something rarely held but deeply wished for.

What Do Naruto's Jutsu Names Actually Mean? 🧵

Every technique you've been yelling has a literal translation

Millions of people spent years yelling "RASENGAN" and "CHIDORI" and "KAGE BUNSHIN NO JUTSU" without knowing what any of those words mean. That's not a problem - that's just how anime absorption works. The phonetics come first. The meaning catches up later.
Rasengan (螺旋丸) means Spiraling Sphere. 螺旋 (rasen) means spiral or helix - the character 螺 depicts a spiral shell, and 旋 means to rotate. 丸 (maru) means sphere or round object.

Chidori (千鳥) means One Thousand Birds. Kakashi named the technique after the crackling sound the electrical current makes as it flows through the arm, which sounded to him like a flock of a thousand birds crying out at once.

Sharingan (写輪眼) means Copy Wheel Eye. 写 (sha) is the character for copy or imitate - the same one used in 写真 (shashin, photograph, literally copying truth). 輪 (rin) means wheel or ring, referring to the spinning tomoe pattern.

The Edo in Edo Tensei (穢土転生) uses completely different kanji from the historical city of Edo (江戸). Edo Tensei uses 穢土, meaning defiled earth or impure land - a Buddhist concept for the world of suffering as opposed to the Pure Land of paradise.

Rinnegan (輪廻眼) means Samsara Eye. 輪廻 (rinne) is the Japanese Buddhist term for samsara - the endless cycle of death, rebirth, and suffering. The same concept appears in 輪廻転生 (rinne tensei), the full phrase for reincarnation. 眼 (gan) means eye.

Kage (影) means shadow, silhouette, or the dark shape cast by something. In Japanese the same word covers both a shadow on the ground and the silhouette of a figure. It is also used metaphorically for a trace or vestige of something that was there.

Why Are Uchiha Jutsus Named After Japanese Gods? 🧵

The Shinto myths hiding inside Naruto's eye powers

When Itachi activates Tsukuyomi from his right eye, that is not a coincidence. When Amaterasu erupts from the left, that is not decoration.

Save this for your next rewatch 📸

Amaterasu (天照) is the Shinto goddess of the sun and ruler of the heavens, one of the most important deities in the Kojiki (712 CE). In the original myth, she was born when the god Izanagi washed his left eye after escaping the underworld.
That is exactly how the original myth works. In the Kojiki, when Izanagi washed his left eye, the sun goddess Amaterasu was born. When he washed his right eye, the moon god Tsukuyomi was born.

The Kojiki (古事記, Record of Ancient Matters) is Japan's oldest chronicle, compiled in 712 CE under Emperor Genmei. It records the creation myth, the age of the gods, and the genealogy of the imperial family.
Susanoo (スサノオ) is the Shinto god of storms, born when Izanagi washed his nose during the same purification ritual that produced Amaterasu and Tsukuyomi.
Izanagi (イザナギ) is the male creator deity of Japanese mythology who helped create the islands of Japan with his wife Izanami.

Bushido: The Samurai Code Running Every Anime You Watch 🧵

武士道 explained - the seven virtues behind Tanjiro's compassion, Zoro's loyalty, and Byakuya's honor

You know that moment when Tanjiro bows to a demon he just killed? When Zoro offers his life to Mihawk without hesitation? When Byakuya executes judgment on someone he loves because duty demands it?

Which of these words have you caught in anime? Reply 👇
Bushido (武士道, literally 'way of the warrior') is the code of moral conduct followed by the Japanese samurai class.

The seven virtues of Bushido are: Gi (義, righteousness/justice), Yu (勇, courage/bravery), Jin (仁, benevolence/compassion), Rei (礼, respect/etiquette), Makoto (誠, honesty/sincerity), Meiyo (名誉, honor/glory), and Chugi (忠義, loyalty/devotion).

The Hagakure (葉隠), written by samurai Yamamoto Tsunetomo around 1716, contains the most famous quote in samurai philosophy: Bushido to wa shinu koto to mitsuketari (武士道とは死ぬことと見つけたり), meaning 'The way of the samurai is found in death.
Tanjiro Kamado from Demon Slayer embodies the Bushido virtue of Jin (仁, benevolence/compassion), showing mercy even toward the demons he kills.

Zoro's entire character is built on Bushido's virtue of Chugi (忠義, loyalty). His absolute loyalty to Luffy, his oath to become the world's greatest swordsman, and his willingness to die for his captain are all classic Bushido values.

Katakana is one of Japan's three writing systems and its main job is to write foreign loanwords. When Japanese borrows a word from English, French, German, or any other language, it is usually written in katakana.
Estimates vary, but Japanese has somewhere between 10,000 and 30,000 words borrowed from English.
Miruku (miruku) is the Japanese loanword for milk, borrowed directly from English and written in katakana as miruku. You will see it on milk cartons, in cafe menus, and in recipes across Japan.
Katakana has 46 base characters and most learners can recognize all of them within a few days of focused practice. The characters look more angular than hiragana, which makes them visually distinct.

Hiragana and katakana both represent the same 46 sounds in Japanese but use different character shapes. Hiragana is rounder and cursive-looking - it is used for native Japanese words and grammatical particles.

Rurouni Kenshin's Japan Was Real 🧵

The samurai who lost everything when the Meiji era began

If you've watched Rurouni Kenshin, you know Kenshin is a wanderer in a Japan that feels like it's moving on without him. Everyone around him is cutting their topknots, wearing Western clothes, building telegraph lines.

Which one surprised you most? Drop it below 👇
Rurouni Kenshin is set in Meiji 11, which is 1878. This is exactly one year after the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877 ended - the last major armed uprising of samurai against the Meiji government.

After 1868, samurai lost their hereditary stipends (abolished by 1876), were forbidden from carrying swords in public by the Haitōrei edict of 1876, and were reclassified as shizoku (warrior families) with no special privileges.
Saigo Takamori, the leader of the Satsuma Rebellion and widely called the last true samurai, is a key historical figure behind the manga's themes.

Saito Hajime was a real historical figure who served as a captain in the Shinsengumi, the elite pro-shogunate sword force. After the Meiji Restoration he reinvented himself as a police officer - exactly as depicted in Rurouni Kenshin. He lived until 1915.
The Haitōrei edict (廃刀令) was a law passed in March 1876 that prohibited anyone except military personnel and police officers from wearing swords in public.

Every Japanese Day of the Week Has an Anime Character in It 🧵

Suicune for Wednesday, Mokuton for Thursday, Light Yagami's secret moon name for Monday - the complete mnemonic map

If you have been memorizing Japanese weekdays as random vocabulary, stop. They are not random. Japanese days of the week are a 1,400-year-old cosmological system, and every single element in that system already has a famous anime character living in it.

The seven days in Japanese are: Nichiyobi (Sunday, 日曜日), Getsuyobi (Monday, 月曜日), Kayobi (Tuesday, 火曜日), Suiyobi (Wednesday, 水曜日), Mokuyobi (Thursday, 木曜日), Kinyobi (Friday, 金曜日), Doyobi (Saturday, 土曜日).

Japanese days of the week are based on the ancient Chinese system of the Seven Luminaries (七曜, shichiyou) - the Sun, Moon, and five classical planets visible to the naked eye (Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn).

Suicune's Japanese name is Suikun (スイクン). The first two syllables, sui (スイ), come from the Japanese word for water, 水 (sui/mizu). This is the same sui in 水曜日 (Suiyobi, Wednesday), which literally means the day of water.
Mokuton (木遁) uses the kanji 木 (moku/ki), meaning wood or tree. Thursday in Japanese is 木曜日 (Mokuyobi), which starts with the same 木 character read the same way: moku.
Light Yagami's Japanese name is written 夜神月 (Yagami Raito). The kanji for his first name is 月, which means moon.

Cha-La Head-Cha-La (チャラ・ヘッチャラ) is a playful nonsense phrase that does not have a literal meaning. The syllables are invented sound play, similar to la-la-la in English.

Cha-La Head-Cha-La is N5-N4 overall, making it one of the most beginner-friendly anime openings. Core vocabulary like genki (energy), uchu (universe), fushigi (mysterious wonder), and tomodachi (friend) is N5-N4.

Why Magikarp Evolves to Gyarados? 🧵

How a 6th-century koi myth became Magikarp's design blueprint

Everyone dunks on Magikarp. Splash. That's it. That's the move. You spend like 20 levels babysitting this useless fish, and the only reason you bother is because you know what's coming.

The Dragon Gate legend (龍門, Ryūmon) is a well-documented Chinese and Japanese folk legend, originating in the Shuijing Zhu (6th century CE). It describes koi climbing a waterfall on the Yellow River and transforming into dragons upon reaching the top.
In the Japanese retelling, demons attracted to the koi's glittering scales would raise the height of the waterfall whenever a fish got close to the top.

Magikarp's Japanese name Koikingu (コイキング) directly references koi (鯉, carp). The mechanic - a long grind with a useless Pokémon that transforms into a powerful dragon - mirrors the koi no takinobori legend directly.

鯉の滝登り (koi no takinobori) means the climbing of the waterfall by the carp. It is a Japanese proverb for achieving something against overwhelming odds, composed of koi (carp), no (possessive particle), taki (waterfall), and nobori (climbing).
In traditional versions the transformed dragon is not given a specific name - it is described as a golden dragon ascending to the heavens.

Itachi (鼬) means weasel. The name IS the word - if you looked up weasel in a Japanese dictionary you would find itachi. Weasels in Japanese folklore are associated with bad omens and death arriving without warning, which fits Itachi Uchiha perfectly.

Strongly so. The lotus (蓮, hasu or ren in Japanese) is one of the most important symbols in Buddhism. It grows rooted in mud at the bottom of ponds but blooms above the water's surface, pure and beautiful.
Tsuyoku nare (強くなれ) means Become stronger or Be strong. Tsuyoku is the adverbial form of tsuyoi (strong, powerful). Nare is the bare imperative of naru (to become). Together: become strong.
Kibou (希望) means hope. The two kanji are ki (希, rare, scarce) and bou (望, wish, desire, gaze). The combination captures something rarely held but deeply wished for.

What Do Naruto's Jutsu Names Actually Mean? 🧵

Every technique you've been yelling has a literal translation

Millions of people spent years yelling "RASENGAN" and "CHIDORI" and "KAGE BUNSHIN NO JUTSU" without knowing what any of those words mean. That's not a problem - that's just how anime absorption works. The phonetics come first. The meaning catches up later.
Rasengan (螺旋丸) means Spiraling Sphere. 螺旋 (rasen) means spiral or helix - the character 螺 depicts a spiral shell, and 旋 means to rotate. 丸 (maru) means sphere or round object.

Chidori (千鳥) means One Thousand Birds. Kakashi named the technique after the crackling sound the electrical current makes as it flows through the arm, which sounded to him like a flock of a thousand birds crying out at once.

Sharingan (写輪眼) means Copy Wheel Eye. 写 (sha) is the character for copy or imitate - the same one used in 写真 (shashin, photograph, literally copying truth). 輪 (rin) means wheel or ring, referring to the spinning tomoe pattern.

The Edo in Edo Tensei (穢土転生) uses completely different kanji from the historical city of Edo (江戸). Edo Tensei uses 穢土, meaning defiled earth or impure land - a Buddhist concept for the world of suffering as opposed to the Pure Land of paradise.

Rinnegan (輪廻眼) means Samsara Eye. 輪廻 (rinne) is the Japanese Buddhist term for samsara - the endless cycle of death, rebirth, and suffering. The same concept appears in 輪廻転生 (rinne tensei), the full phrase for reincarnation. 眼 (gan) means eye.

The Shinto myths hiding inside Naruto's eye powers

Amaterasu (天照) is the Shinto goddess of the sun and ruler of the heavens, one of the most important deities in the Kojiki (712 CE). In the original myth, she was born when the god Izanagi washed his left eye after escaping the underworld.
That is exactly how the original myth works. In the Kojiki, when Izanagi washed his left eye, the sun goddess Amaterasu was born. When he washed his right eye, the moon god Tsukuyomi was born.

The Kojiki (古事記, Record of Ancient Matters) is Japan's oldest chronicle, compiled in 712 CE under Emperor Genmei. It records the creation myth, the age of the gods, and the genealogy of the imperial family.
Susanoo (スサノオ) is the Shinto god of storms, born when Izanagi washed his nose during the same purification ritual that produced Amaterasu and Tsukuyomi.
Izanagi (イザナギ) is the male creator deity of Japanese mythology who helped create the islands of Japan with his wife Izanami.

Bushido: The Samurai Code Running Every Anime You Watch 🧵

武士道 explained - the seven virtues behind Tanjiro's compassion, Zoro's loyalty, and Byakuya's honor

You know that moment when Tanjiro bows to a demon he just killed? When Zoro offers his life to Mihawk without hesitation? When Byakuya executes judgment on someone he loves because duty demands it?

Which of these words have you caught in anime? Reply 👇
Bushido (武士道, literally 'way of the warrior') is the code of moral conduct followed by the Japanese samurai class.

The seven virtues of Bushido are: Gi (義, righteousness/justice), Yu (勇, courage/bravery), Jin (仁, benevolence/compassion), Rei (礼, respect/etiquette), Makoto (誠, honesty/sincerity), Meiyo (名誉, honor/glory), and Chugi (忠義, loyalty/devotion).

The Hagakure (葉隠), written by samurai Yamamoto Tsunetomo around 1716, contains the most famous quote in samurai philosophy: Bushido to wa shinu koto to mitsuketari (武士道とは死ぬことと見つけたり), meaning 'The way of the samurai is found in death.
Tanjiro Kamado from Demon Slayer embodies the Bushido virtue of Jin (仁, benevolence/compassion), showing mercy even toward the demons he kills.

Zoro's entire character is built on Bushido's virtue of Chugi (忠義, loyalty). His absolute loyalty to Luffy, his oath to become the world's greatest swordsman, and his willingness to die for his captain are all classic Bushido values.

Katakana is one of Japan's three writing systems and its main job is to write foreign loanwords. When Japanese borrows a word from English, French, German, or any other language, it is usually written in katakana.
Estimates vary, but Japanese has somewhere between 10,000 and 30,000 words borrowed from English.
Miruku (miruku) is the Japanese loanword for milk, borrowed directly from English and written in katakana as miruku. You will see it on milk cartons, in cafe menus, and in recipes across Japan.
Katakana has 46 base characters and most learners can recognize all of them within a few days of focused practice. The characters look more angular than hiragana, which makes them visually distinct.

Hiragana and katakana both represent the same 46 sounds in Japanese but use different character shapes. Hiragana is rounder and cursive-looking - it is used for native Japanese words and grammatical particles.

Rurouni Kenshin's Japan Was Real 🧵

The samurai who lost everything when the Meiji era began

If you've watched Rurouni Kenshin, you know Kenshin is a wanderer in a Japan that feels like it's moving on without him. Everyone around him is cutting their topknots, wearing Western clothes, building telegraph lines.

Which one surprised you most? Drop it below 👇
Rurouni Kenshin is set in Meiji 11, which is 1878. This is exactly one year after the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877 ended - the last major armed uprising of samurai against the Meiji government.

After 1868, samurai lost their hereditary stipends (abolished by 1876), were forbidden from carrying swords in public by the Haitōrei edict of 1876, and were reclassified as shizoku (warrior families) with no special privileges.
Saigo Takamori, the leader of the Satsuma Rebellion and widely called the last true samurai, is a key historical figure behind the manga's themes.

Saito Hajime was a real historical figure who served as a captain in the Shinsengumi, the elite pro-shogunate sword force. After the Meiji Restoration he reinvented himself as a police officer - exactly as depicted in Rurouni Kenshin. He lived until 1915.
The Haitōrei edict (廃刀令) was a law passed in March 1876 that prohibited anyone except military personnel and police officers from wearing swords in public.

Is Oden From One Piece Based on a Real Person? 🧵

The Sengoku warlords hiding inside Wano's most legendary samurai

You remember the scene. Oden standing in the boiling oil, holding his retainers above his head, counting down the minutes. That final speech. I am Kozuki Oden, and I was born to boil.

Not on a single real person, but on a synthesis of several Sengoku-era historical figures. His betrayal and death most closely mirror Oda Nobunaga, who was killed by his own retainer Akechi Mitsuhide at Honnoji in 1582.

Oden (おでん) is a real Japanese hot pot dish made of simmered ingredients like daikon, tofu, and fish cakes. Eiichiro Oda names many characters in Wano Country after Japanese food: Orochi, Kaido's retainers, and others all carry food-based names.
Boiling as an execution method existed in Japanese history, particularly in the Edo period (1603-1868). The practice was called jigoku-ni, meaning hell boiling.
Bushido (武士道, the way of the warrior) is the samurai code of ethics emphasizing loyalty, honor, and accepting death with dignity.
The Honnoji incident (1582) is when the powerful warlord Oda Nobunaga was betrayed by his own retainer Akechi Mitsuhide and killed.

Every Japanese Day of the Week Has an Anime Character in It 🧵

Suicune for Wednesday, Mokuton for Thursday, Light Yagami's secret moon name for Monday - the complete mnemonic map

If you have been memorizing Japanese weekdays as random vocabulary, stop. They are not random. Japanese days of the week are a 1,400-year-old cosmological system, and every single element in that system already has a famous anime character living in it.

The seven days in Japanese are: Nichiyobi (Sunday, 日曜日), Getsuyobi (Monday, 月曜日), Kayobi (Tuesday, 火曜日), Suiyobi (Wednesday, 水曜日), Mokuyobi (Thursday, 木曜日), Kinyobi (Friday, 金曜日), Doyobi (Saturday, 土曜日).

Japanese days of the week are based on the ancient Chinese system of the Seven Luminaries (七曜, shichiyou) - the Sun, Moon, and five classical planets visible to the naked eye (Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn).

Suicune's Japanese name is Suikun (スイクン). The first two syllables, sui (スイ), come from the Japanese word for water, 水 (sui/mizu). This is the same sui in 水曜日 (Suiyobi, Wednesday), which literally means the day of water.
Mokuton (木遁) uses the kanji 木 (moku/ki), meaning wood or tree. Thursday in Japanese is 木曜日 (Mokuyobi), which starts with the same 木 character read the same way: moku.
Light Yagami's Japanese name is written 夜神月 (Yagami Raito). The kanji for his first name is 月, which means moon.

Ninja vs Samurai: They Were Never the Same Thing 🧵

The class war hiding inside every anime you've ever watched

Save this for your next rewatch 📸

Ninja - properly called shinobi (忍び) - were documented historical operatives active primarily during Japan's Sengoku era (roughly 1467-1615). The Iga and Koka provinces of central Japan produced the most famous schools of ninjutsu.
Shinobi (忍び) means one who endures or one who steals away. The character 忍 combines 刃 (blade) over 心 (heart) - a blade over the heart, representing the endurance required to operate in secret.
Samurai (侍) were Japan's official aristocratic warrior class - military nobility with a recognized social rank, a legal code, and the right to carry two swords.
- Naruto is fantastical and mythologized. Real ninjutsu had no chakra system, no elemental transformations, and no giant summoned animals.

Not explicitly, but structurally yes. The Demon Slayer Corps operates on samurai ethical principles without naming them: absolute loyalty to the mission, protection of innocents, acceptance of death over retreat, and respect for enemies.

How a 6th-century koi myth became Magikarp's design blueprint

The Dragon Gate legend (龍門, Ryūmon) is a well-documented Chinese and Japanese folk legend, originating in the Shuijing Zhu (6th century CE). It describes koi climbing a waterfall on the Yellow River and transforming into dragons upon reaching the top.
In the Japanese retelling, demons attracted to the koi's glittering scales would raise the height of the waterfall whenever a fish got close to the top.

Magikarp's Japanese name Koikingu (コイキング) directly references koi (鯉, carp). The mechanic - a long grind with a useless Pokémon that transforms into a powerful dragon - mirrors the koi no takinobori legend directly.

鯉の滝登り (koi no takinobori) means the climbing of the waterfall by the carp. It is a Japanese proverb for achieving something against overwhelming odds, composed of koi (carp), no (possessive particle), taki (waterfall), and nobori (climbing).
In traditional versions the transformed dragon is not given a specific name - it is described as a golden dragon ascending to the heavens.

Inuyasha (犬夜叉) starts with inu (犬), which means dog. Inu is one of the first animal words in Japanese and shows up everywhere - Shiba Inu, Inuzuka clan, Akita Inu. His name literally begins with the word for dog because he is half-dog demon.

The word Saiyan (サイヤ人, Saiyajin) is itself an anagram of yasai (野菜), the Japanese word for vegetables. The whole race is a vegetable pun. Vegeta is obviously vegetable, and Gohan - Goku's son - is the Japanese word for cooked rice.

Kakashi (案山子) literally means scarecrow. It is not a metaphor - that is the actual Japanese dictionary word for a scarecrow. Whenever you hear kakashi, think of the straw figure in the field. That image will lock the word in permanently.

Ichigo sounds exactly like the Japanese word for strawberry (苺, ichigo). Tite Kubo made this a deliberate pun - Ichigo's hair is orange like a strawberry, but his name kanji (一護) means the one who protects.

Itachi (鼬) means weasel. The name IS the word - if you looked up weasel in a Japanese dictionary you would find itachi. Weasels in Japanese folklore are associated with bad omens and death arriving without warning, which fits Itachi Uchiha perfectly.

Captain Tsubasa (キャプテン翼) is a manga and anime series by Yoichi Takahashi, first published in Weekly Shonen Jump in 1981. It follows Tsubasa Ozora, a boy obsessed with soccer, from youth football in Japan through international competition.
Widely credited so. Multiple Japanese football stars including Hidetoshi Nakata have cited Captain Tsubasa as the reason they started playing. The series launched 12 years before the J.
The main teams are fictional youth clubs: Nankatsu SC (Tsubasa's home team), Musashi FC (rival Hyuga's team), Shutetsu FC, and Toho Academy (Hyuga's high school club).

Karl Heinz Schneider is clearly based on Karl-Heinz Rummenigge (West Germany), Pierre is based on Michel Platini (France), and various Brazilian and Italian characters reference real players from the 1980s.

Zico (real name Artur Antunes Coimbra) is a Brazilian legend and one of the greatest footballers of all time. He signed for Sumitomo Metals (later renamed Kashima Antlers) in 1991, two years before the J.League launched.

三代目 (sandaime) means the third-generation holder of the Hokage title. 三 (san) = 3, 代 (dai) = generation or succession, 目 (me) = ordinal suffix that turns a number into nth. The Third Hokage, Hiruzen Sarutobi, holds this title.

三人 (sannin) literally means three people. 三 (san) = 3, 人 (nin) = person or people counter. The legendary Sannin - Jiraiya, Tsunade, and Orochimaru - are simply the three people at the apex of Konoha's shinobi.

四皇 (Yonko) means Four Emperors. 四 (yon) = 4, 皇 (ko) = emperor. The four most powerful pirates who dominate the New World. The number is literally encoded in the title - if you know yon equals 4, the faction name tells you exactly how many there are.
七代目 (nanadaime) means the seventh-generation Hokage. 七 (nana) = 7, 代目 (daime) = nth-generation holder of a title. Naruto Uzumaki is the Nanadaime Hokage, the seventh person to hold the title.
七つ (nanatsu) is the native Japanese reading of 7, from the older counting system (hitotsu, futatsu, mittsu...). 七 (shichi) is the Sino-Japanese reading.

Learning Japanese with Homura (Demon Slayer: Mugen Train Theme) 🧵

Tamashii, kienai, and the Japanese vocabulary for what survives after someone is gone

If you saw Demon Slayer: Mugen Train in theatres, you know exactly when Homura starts playing and what happens when it does. The end of one of the most devastating moments in recent anime history, and then LiSA's voice comes in. You were not ready.

Homura (炎) means flame or fire in Japanese. The single kanji 炎 is the elevated literary form of fire, distinct from the more common 火 (hi, ordinary fire/flame). 炎 specifically suggests intense, upward-burning flame with a sense of power and spiritual presence.
Homura is N3-N2 in places, with pockets of N4 vocabulary. Key words like tamashii (soul/spirit), kienai (won't disappear/undying), inochi (life), and tsuyoku (strongly) are N3-N4.
Homura (炎) is performed by LiSA (Risa Oribe). The title means flame - specifically the archaic, poetic reading of the kanji 炎 that evokes intense spiritual fire.
Tamashii (魂) means soul, spirit, or essence - the deepest inner core of a person that persists beyond their physical existence.

Kienai (消えない) means won't disappear, undying, unfading. It combines kieru (消える, to disappear, to go out - used for flames, lights, and presences) with the negative nai (ない). So kienai is the negative of a flame going out: a flame that won't die.

What Do Naruto's Jutsu Names Actually Mean? 🧵

Every technique you've been yelling has a literal translation

Millions of people spent years yelling "RASENGAN" and "CHIDORI" and "KAGE BUNSHIN NO JUTSU" without knowing what any of those words mean. That's not a problem - that's just how anime absorption works. The phonetics come first. The meaning catches up later.
Rasengan (螺旋丸) means Spiraling Sphere. 螺旋 (rasen) means spiral or helix - the character 螺 depicts a spiral shell, and 旋 means to rotate. 丸 (maru) means sphere or round object.

Chidori (千鳥) means One Thousand Birds. Kakashi named the technique after the crackling sound the electrical current makes as it flows through the arm, which sounded to him like a flock of a thousand birds crying out at once.

Sharingan (写輪眼) means Copy Wheel Eye. 写 (sha) is the character for copy or imitate - the same one used in 写真 (shashin, photograph, literally copying truth). 輪 (rin) means wheel or ring, referring to the spinning tomoe pattern.

The Edo in Edo Tensei (穢土転生) uses completely different kanji from the historical city of Edo (江戸). Edo Tensei uses 穢土, meaning defiled earth or impure land - a Buddhist concept for the world of suffering as opposed to the Pure Land of paradise.

Rinnegan (輪廻眼) means Samsara Eye. 輪廻 (rinne) is the Japanese Buddhist term for samsara - the endless cycle of death, rebirth, and suffering. The same concept appears in 輪廻転生 (rinne tensei), the full phrase for reincarnation. 眼 (gan) means eye.

Kage (影) means shadow, silhouette, or the dark shape cast by something. In Japanese the same word covers both a shadow on the ground and the silhouette of a figure. It is also used metaphorically for a trace or vestige of something that was there.

The Shinto myths hiding inside Naruto's eye powers

Amaterasu (天照) is the Shinto goddess of the sun and ruler of the heavens, one of the most important deities in the Kojiki (712 CE). In the original myth, she was born when the god Izanagi washed his left eye after escaping the underworld.
That is exactly how the original myth works. In the Kojiki, when Izanagi washed his left eye, the sun goddess Amaterasu was born. When he washed his right eye, the moon god Tsukuyomi was born.

The Kojiki (古事記, Record of Ancient Matters) is Japan's oldest chronicle, compiled in 712 CE under Emperor Genmei. It records the creation myth, the age of the gods, and the genealogy of the imperial family.
Susanoo (スサノオ) is the Shinto god of storms, born when Izanagi washed his nose during the same purification ritual that produced Amaterasu and Tsukuyomi.
Izanagi (イザナギ) is the male creator deity of Japanese mythology who helped create the islands of Japan with his wife Izanami.

Bushido (武士道, literally 'way of the warrior') is the code of moral conduct followed by the Japanese samurai class.

The seven virtues of Bushido are: Gi (義, righteousness/justice), Yu (勇, courage/bravery), Jin (仁, benevolence/compassion), Rei (礼, respect/etiquette), Makoto (誠, honesty/sincerity), Meiyo (名誉, honor/glory), and Chugi (忠義, loyalty/devotion).

The Hagakure (葉隠), written by samurai Yamamoto Tsunetomo around 1716, contains the most famous quote in samurai philosophy: Bushido to wa shinu koto to mitsuketari (武士道とは死ぬことと見つけたり), meaning 'The way of the samurai is found in death.
Tanjiro Kamado from Demon Slayer embodies the Bushido virtue of Jin (仁, benevolence/compassion), showing mercy even toward the demons he kills.

Zoro's entire character is built on Bushido's virtue of Chugi (忠義, loyalty). His absolute loyalty to Luffy, his oath to become the world's greatest swordsman, and his willingness to die for his captain are all classic Bushido values.

Katakana is one of Japan's three writing systems and its main job is to write foreign loanwords. When Japanese borrows a word from English, French, German, or any other language, it is usually written in katakana.
Estimates vary, but Japanese has somewhere between 10,000 and 30,000 words borrowed from English.
Miruku (miruku) is the Japanese loanword for milk, borrowed directly from English and written in katakana as miruku. You will see it on milk cartons, in cafe menus, and in recipes across Japan.
Katakana has 46 base characters and most learners can recognize all of them within a few days of focused practice. The characters look more angular than hiragana, which makes them visually distinct.

Hiragana and katakana both represent the same 46 sounds in Japanese but use different character shapes. Hiragana is rounder and cursive-looking - it is used for native Japanese words and grammatical particles.

Rurouni Kenshin's Japan Was Real 🧵

The samurai who lost everything when the Meiji era began

If you've watched Rurouni Kenshin, you know Kenshin is a wanderer in a Japan that feels like it's moving on without him. Everyone around him is cutting their topknots, wearing Western clothes, building telegraph lines.

Which one surprised you most? Drop it below 👇
Rurouni Kenshin is set in Meiji 11, which is 1878. This is exactly one year after the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877 ended - the last major armed uprising of samurai against the Meiji government.

After 1868, samurai lost their hereditary stipends (abolished by 1876), were forbidden from carrying swords in public by the Haitōrei edict of 1876, and were reclassified as shizoku (warrior families) with no special privileges.
Saigo Takamori, the leader of the Satsuma Rebellion and widely called the last true samurai, is a key historical figure behind the manga's themes.

Saito Hajime was a real historical figure who served as a captain in the Shinsengumi, the elite pro-shogunate sword force. After the Meiji Restoration he reinvented himself as a police officer - exactly as depicted in Rurouni Kenshin. He lived until 1915.
The Haitōrei edict (廃刀令) was a law passed in March 1876 that prohibited anyone except military personnel and police officers from wearing swords in public.

Oden (おでん) is a real Japanese hot pot dish made of simmered ingredients like daikon, tofu, and fish cakes. Eiichiro Oda names many characters in Wano Country after Japanese food: Orochi, Kaido's retainers, and others all carry food-based names.

Bushido (武士道, the way of the warrior) is the samurai code of ethics emphasizing loyalty, honor, and accepting death with dignity.
The Honnoji incident (1582) is when the powerful warlord Oda Nobunaga was betrayed by his own retainer Akechi Mitsuhide and killed.

Every Japanese Day of the Week Has an Anime Character in It 🧵

Suicune for Wednesday, Mokuton for Thursday, Light Yagami's secret moon name for Monday - the complete mnemonic map

If you have been memorizing Japanese weekdays as random vocabulary, stop. They are not random. Japanese days of the week are a 1,400-year-old cosmological system, and every single element in that system already has a famous anime character living in it.

The seven days in Japanese are: Nichiyobi (Sunday, 日曜日), Getsuyobi (Monday, 月曜日), Kayobi (Tuesday, 火曜日), Suiyobi (Wednesday, 水曜日), Mokuyobi (Thursday, 木曜日), Kinyobi (Friday, 金曜日), Doyobi (Saturday, 土曜日).

Japanese days of the week are based on the ancient Chinese system of the Seven Luminaries (七曜, shichiyou) - the Sun, Moon, and five classical planets visible to the naked eye (Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn).

Suicune's Japanese name is Suikun (スイクン). The first two syllables, sui (スイ), come from the Japanese word for water, 水 (sui/mizu). This is the same sui in 水曜日 (Suiyobi, Wednesday), which literally means the day of water.
Mokuton (木遁) uses the kanji 木 (moku/ki), meaning wood or tree. Thursday in Japanese is 木曜日 (Mokuyobi), which starts with the same 木 character read the same way: moku.
Light Yagami's Japanese name is written 夜神月 (Yagami Raito). The kanji for his first name is 月, which means moon.

The class war hiding inside every anime you've ever watched

If you grew up watching Naruto, you probably thought ninja and samurai were just two flavors of the same cool Japanese fighter. Both had swords (or sword-adjacent weapons). Both had intense training. Both popped up in period anime.

Ninja - properly called shinobi (忍び) - were documented historical operatives active primarily during Japan's Sengoku era (roughly 1467-1615). The Iga and Koka provinces of central Japan produced the most famous schools of ninjutsu.
Shinobi (忍び) means one who endures or one who steals away. The character 忍 combines 刃 (blade) over 心 (heart) - a blade over the heart, representing the endurance required to operate in secret.
Samurai (侍) were Japan's official aristocratic warrior class - military nobility with a recognized social rank, a legal code, and the right to carry two swords.
- Naruto is fantastical and mythologized. Real ninjutsu had no chakra system, no elemental transformations, and no giant summoned animals.

Not explicitly, but structurally yes. The Demon Slayer Corps operates on samurai ethical principles without naming them: absolute loyalty to the mission, protection of innocents, acceptance of death over retreat, and respect for enemies.

Why Magikarp Evolves to Gyarados? 🧵

How a 6th-century koi myth became Magikarp's design blueprint

Everyone dunks on Magikarp. Splash. That's it. That's the move. You spend like 20 levels babysitting this useless fish, and the only reason you bother is because you know what's coming.

Save this for your next rewatch 📸

The Dragon Gate legend (龍門, Ryūmon) is a well-documented Chinese and Japanese folk legend, originating in the Shuijing Zhu (6th century CE). It describes koi climbing a waterfall on the Yellow River and transforming into dragons upon reaching the top.
In the Japanese retelling, demons attracted to the koi's glittering scales would raise the height of the waterfall whenever a fish got close to the top.

Magikarp's Japanese name Koikingu (コイキング) directly references koi (鯉, carp). The mechanic - a long grind with a useless Pokémon that transforms into a powerful dragon - mirrors the koi no takinobori legend directly.

鯉の滝登り (koi no takinobori) means the climbing of the waterfall by the carp. It is a Japanese proverb for achieving something against overwhelming odds, composed of koi (carp), no (possessive particle), taki (waterfall), and nobori (climbing).
In traditional versions the transformed dragon is not given a specific name - it is described as a golden dragon ascending to the heavens.

You have watched hundreds of episodes of anime, absorbed dozens of character names, and if you knew Japanese, you would have been learning vocabulary every single time someone said a name out loud.

Save this for your next rewatch 📸

Inuyasha (犬夜叉) starts with inu (犬), which means dog. Inu is one of the first animal words in Japanese and shows up everywhere - Shiba Inu, Inuzuka clan, Akita Inu. His name literally begins with the word for dog because he is half-dog demon.

The word Saiyan (サイヤ人, Saiyajin) is itself an anagram of yasai (野菜), the Japanese word for vegetables. The whole race is a vegetable pun. Vegeta is obviously vegetable, and Gohan - Goku's son - is the Japanese word for cooked rice.

Kakashi (案山子) literally means scarecrow. It is not a metaphor - that is the actual Japanese dictionary word for a scarecrow. Whenever you hear kakashi, think of the straw figure in the field. That image will lock the word in permanently.

Ichigo sounds exactly like the Japanese word for strawberry (苺, ichigo). Tite Kubo made this a deliberate pun - Ichigo's hair is orange like a strawberry, but his name kanji (一護) means the one who protects.

Itachi (鼬) means weasel. The name IS the word - if you looked up weasel in a Japanese dictionary you would find itachi. Weasels in Japanese folklore are associated with bad omens and death arriving without warning, which fits Itachi Uchiha perfectly.

The manga, the Brazilian legend who played in Japan, and how an entire nation caught football fever

In 1981, Japan was a country where baseball was king, sumo was sacred, and soccer was a distant afterthought that corporate employees played on weekends for their company teams. Nobody was watching. Nobody cared.

Which one surprised you most? Drop it below 👇

Captain Tsubasa (キャプテン翼) is a manga and anime series by Yoichi Takahashi, first published in Weekly Shonen Jump in 1981. It follows Tsubasa Ozora, a boy obsessed with soccer, from youth football in Japan through international competition.
Widely credited so. Multiple Japanese football stars including Hidetoshi Nakata have cited Captain Tsubasa as the reason they started playing. The series launched 12 years before the J.
The main teams are fictional youth clubs: Nankatsu SC (Tsubasa's home team), Musashi FC (rival Hyuga's team), Shutetsu FC, and Toho Academy (Hyuga's high school club).

Karl Heinz Schneider is clearly based on Karl-Heinz Rummenigge (West Germany), Pierre is based on Michel Platini (France), and various Brazilian and Italian characters reference real players from the 1980s.

Zico (real name Artur Antunes Coimbra) is a Brazilian legend and one of the greatest footballers of all time. He signed for Sumitomo Metals (later renamed Kashima Antlers) in 1991, two years before the J.League launched.

The hodo pattern, lotus symbolism, and what 'hope seized with trembling hands' really means

When Gurenge dropped as the Demon Slayer opening in 2019, most anime fans just knew it as an absolutely relentless hype track.

Save this for your next rewatch 📸
Gurenge (紅蓮華) means Red Lotus Flower. The kanji compound is made of three characters: gu (紅, crimson or deep red), ren (蓮, lotus plant), and ge (華, flower, blossom).

Gurenge is intermediate difficulty - mostly N4 to N3. The core vocabulary (yume for dream, kibou for hope, tsuyoku for strongly) is N4. Grammar patterns like hodo (the more X, the more Y) and tame ni (for the sake of) are N4.

Strongly so. The lotus (蓮, hasu or ren in Japanese) is one of the most important symbols in Buddhism. It grows rooted in mud at the bottom of ponds but blooms above the water's surface, pure and beautiful.
Tsuyoku nare (強くなれ) means Become stronger or Be strong. Tsuyoku is the adverbial form of tsuyoi (strong, powerful). Nare is the bare imperative of naru (to become). Together: become strong.
Kibou (希望) means hope. The two kanji are ki (希, rare, scarce) and bou (望, wish, desire, gaze). The combination captures something rarely held but deeply wished for.

You Already Know How to Count in Japanese 🧵

Hokage titles, Yonko, and Sannin have been teaching you Japanese numbers all along

Every time you called Minato "the Yondaime" you said four. Every time someone referenced the Sannin you said three. Every time you talked about the Yonko era in One Piece you said four again.

Which of these words have you caught in anime? Reply 👇

三代目 (sandaime) means the third-generation holder of the Hokage title. 三 (san) = 3, 代 (dai) = generation or succession, 目 (me) = ordinal suffix that turns a number into nth. The Third Hokage, Hiruzen Sarutobi, holds this title.

三人 (sannin) literally means three people. 三 (san) = 3, 人 (nin) = person or people counter. The legendary Sannin - Jiraiya, Tsunade, and Orochimaru - are simply the three people at the apex of Konoha's shinobi.

四皇 (Yonko) means Four Emperors. 四 (yon) = 4, 皇 (ko) = emperor. The four most powerful pirates who dominate the New World. The number is literally encoded in the title - if you know yon equals 4, the faction name tells you exactly how many there are.
七代目 (nanadaime) means the seventh-generation Hokage. 七 (nana) = 7, 代目 (daime) = nth-generation holder of a title. Naruto Uzumaki is the Nanadaime Hokage, the seventh person to hold the title.
七つ (nanatsu) is the native Japanese reading of 7, from the older counting system (hitotsu, futatsu, mittsu...). 七 (shichi) is the Sino-Japanese reading.

Learning Japanese with Homura (Demon Slayer: Mugen Train Theme) 🧵

Tamashii, kienai, and the Japanese vocabulary for what survives after someone is gone

If you saw Demon Slayer: Mugen Train in theatres, you know exactly when Homura starts playing and what happens when it does. The end of one of the most devastating moments in recent anime history, and then LiSA's voice comes in. You were not ready.

Homura (炎) means flame or fire in Japanese. The single kanji 炎 is the elevated literary form of fire, distinct from the more common 火 (hi, ordinary fire/flame). 炎 specifically suggests intense, upward-burning flame with a sense of power and spiritual presence.
Homura is N3-N2 in places, with pockets of N4 vocabulary. Key words like tamashii (soul/spirit), kienai (won't disappear/undying), inochi (life), and tsuyoku (strongly) are N3-N4.
Homura (炎) is performed by LiSA (Risa Oribe). The title means flame - specifically the archaic, poetic reading of the kanji 炎 that evokes intense spiritual fire.
Tamashii (魂) means soul, spirit, or essence - the deepest inner core of a person that persists beyond their physical existence.

Kienai (消えない) means won't disappear, undying, unfading. It combines kieru (消える, to disappear, to go out - used for flames, lights, and presences) with the negative nai (ない). So kienai is the negative of a flame going out: a flame that won't die.

What Do Naruto's Jutsu Names Actually Mean? 🧵

Every technique you've been yelling has a literal translation

Millions of people spent years yelling "RASENGAN" and "CHIDORI" and "KAGE BUNSHIN NO JUTSU" without knowing what any of those words mean. That's not a problem - that's just how anime absorption works. The phonetics come first. The meaning catches up later.
Rasengan (螺旋丸) means Spiraling Sphere. 螺旋 (rasen) means spiral or helix - the character 螺 depicts a spiral shell, and 旋 means to rotate. 丸 (maru) means sphere or round object.

Chidori (千鳥) means One Thousand Birds. Kakashi named the technique after the crackling sound the electrical current makes as it flows through the arm, which sounded to him like a flock of a thousand birds crying out at once.

Sharingan (写輪眼) means Copy Wheel Eye. 写 (sha) is the character for copy or imitate - the same one used in 写真 (shashin, photograph, literally copying truth). 輪 (rin) means wheel or ring, referring to the spinning tomoe pattern.

The Edo in Edo Tensei (穢土転生) uses completely different kanji from the historical city of Edo (江戸). Edo Tensei uses 穢土, meaning defiled earth or impure land - a Buddhist concept for the world of suffering as opposed to the Pure Land of paradise.

Rinnegan (輪廻眼) means Samsara Eye. 輪廻 (rinne) is the Japanese Buddhist term for samsara - the endless cycle of death, rebirth, and suffering. The same concept appears in 輪廻転生 (rinne tensei), the full phrase for reincarnation. 眼 (gan) means eye.

Oikakeru, kage, and how te iku encodes the direction that Sasuke is always going

Which of these words have you caught in anime? Reply 👇

Silhouette is written in katakana as シルエット (shirueetto) in Japanese, where it is used with the same meaning as in English: the dark outline or shadow-shape of a figure seen against a lighter background.
Silhouette sits at N4 overall, making it accessible to intermediate beginners. Core vocabulary like kage (shadow), oikakeru (to chase after), and hashiru (to run) is N4-N3.

Silhouette is performed by KANA-BOON, a Japanese rock band from Osaka formed in 2008. The band consists of Maguro Taniguchi (vocals, guitar), Ryusei Kiuchi (guitar), Hiroyuki Motoyama (bass), and Yoshiya Okamoto (drums).

Oikakeru (追いかける) means to chase after, to pursue, to run after someone or something. It is a compound verb: oi (追い, the combining form of 追う, to chase) + kakeru (駆ける, to run, to race). Together: to run in pursuit of someone.

Kage (影) means shadow, silhouette, or the dark shape cast by something. In Japanese the same word covers both a shadow on the ground and the silhouette of a figure. It is also used metaphorically for a trace or vestige of something that was there.

Why Are Uchiha Jutsus Named After Japanese Gods? 🧵

The Shinto myths hiding inside Naruto's eye powers

When Itachi activates Tsukuyomi from his right eye, that is not a coincidence. When Amaterasu erupts from the left, that is not decoration.

Did you already know any of these? Reply 👇

Amaterasu (天照) is the Shinto goddess of the sun and ruler of the heavens, one of the most important deities in the Kojiki (712 CE). In the original myth, she was born when the god Izanagi washed his left eye after escaping the underworld.
That is exactly how the original myth works. In the Kojiki, when Izanagi washed his left eye, the sun goddess Amaterasu was born. When he washed his right eye, the moon god Tsukuyomi was born.

The Kojiki (古事記, Record of Ancient Matters) is Japan's oldest chronicle, compiled in 712 CE under Emperor Genmei. It records the creation myth, the age of the gods, and the genealogy of the imperial family.
Susanoo (スサノオ) is the Shinto god of storms, born when Izanagi washed his nose during the same purification ritual that produced Amaterasu and Tsukuyomi.
Izanagi (イザナギ) is the male creator deity of Japanese mythology who helped create the islands of Japan with his wife Izanami.

Bushido (武士道, literally 'way of the warrior') is the code of moral conduct followed by the Japanese samurai class.

The Hagakure (葉隠), written by samurai Yamamoto Tsunetomo around 1716, contains the most famous quote in samurai philosophy: Bushido to wa shinu koto to mitsuketari (武士道とは死ぬことと見つけたり), meaning 'The way of the samurai is found in death.
Tanjiro Kamado from Demon Slayer embodies the Bushido virtue of Jin (仁, benevolence/compassion), showing mercy even toward the demons he kills.

Zoro's entire character is built on Bushido's virtue of Chugi (忠義, loyalty). His absolute loyalty to Luffy, his oath to become the world's greatest swordsman, and his willingness to die for his captain are all classic Bushido values.

Katakana is one of Japan's three writing systems and its main job is to write foreign loanwords. When Japanese borrows a word from English, French, German, or any other language, it is usually written in katakana.

Rurouni Kenshin's Japan Was Real 🧵

The samurai who lost everything when the Meiji era began

If you've watched Rurouni Kenshin, you know Kenshin is a wanderer in a Japan that feels like it's moving on without him. Everyone around him is cutting their topknots, wearing Western clothes, building telegraph lines.

Did you already know any of these? Reply 👇
Rurouni Kenshin is set in Meiji 11, which is 1878. This is exactly one year after the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877 ended - the last major armed uprising of samurai against the Meiji government.

After 1868, samurai lost their hereditary stipends (abolished by 1876), were forbidden from carrying swords in public by the Haitōrei edict of 1876, and were reclassified as shizoku (warrior families) with no special privileges.
Saigo Takamori, the leader of the Satsuma Rebellion and widely called the last true samurai, is a key historical figure behind the manga's themes.

Saito Hajime was a real historical figure who served as a captain in the Shinsengumi, the elite pro-shogunate sword force. After the Meiji Restoration he reinvented himself as a police officer - exactly as depicted in Rurouni Kenshin. He lived until 1915.
The Haitōrei edict (廃刀令) was a law passed in March 1876 that prohibited anyone except military personnel and police officers from wearing swords in public.

Every Japanese Day of the Week Has an Anime Character in It 🧵

Suicune for Wednesday, Mokuton for Thursday, Light Yagami's secret moon name for Monday - the complete mnemonic map

If you have been memorizing Japanese weekdays as random vocabulary, stop. They are not random. Japanese days of the week are a 1,400-year-old cosmological system, and every single element in that system already has a famous anime character living in it.

The seven days in Japanese are: Nichiyobi (Sunday, 日曜日), Getsuyobi (Monday, 月曜日), Kayobi (Tuesday, 火曜日), Suiyobi (Wednesday, 水曜日), Mokuyobi (Thursday, 木曜日), Kinyobi (Friday, 金曜日), Doyobi (Saturday, 土曜日).

Japanese days of the week are based on the ancient Chinese system of the Seven Luminaries (七曜, shichiyou) - the Sun, Moon, and five classical planets visible to the naked eye (Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn).

Suicune's Japanese name is Suikun (スイクン). The first two syllables, sui (スイ), come from the Japanese word for water, 水 (sui/mizu). This is the same sui in 水曜日 (Suiyobi, Wednesday), which literally means the day of water.
Mokuton (木遁) uses the kanji 木 (moku/ki), meaning wood or tree. Thursday in Japanese is 木曜日 (Mokuyobi), which starts with the same 木 character read the same way: moku.
Light Yagami's Japanese name is written 夜神月 (Yagami Raito). The kanji for his first name is 月, which means moon.

Fushigi (不思議) means mysterious, wondrous, strange, or inexplicable - something that defies normal understanding. The kanji: fu (不, not) + shi (思, think) + gi (議, discuss/reason). Literally: something that cannot be reasoned about, beyond discussion.

Ninja vs Samurai: They Were Never the Same Thing 🧵

The class war hiding inside every anime you've ever watched

If you grew up watching Naruto, you probably thought ninja and samurai were just two flavors of the same cool Japanese fighter. Both had swords (or sword-adjacent weapons). Both had intense training. Both popped up in period anime.

Ninja - properly called shinobi (忍び) - were documented historical operatives active primarily during Japan's Sengoku era (roughly 1467-1615). The Iga and Koka provinces of central Japan produced the most famous schools of ninjutsu.
Shinobi (忍び) means one who endures or one who steals away. The character 忍 combines 刃 (blade) over 心 (heart) - a blade over the heart, representing the endurance required to operate in secret.
Samurai (侍) were Japan's official aristocratic warrior class - military nobility with a recognized social rank, a legal code, and the right to carry two swords.
- Naruto is fantastical and mythologized. Real ninjutsu had no chakra system, no elemental transformations, and no giant summoned animals.

Not explicitly, but structurally yes. The Demon Slayer Corps operates on samurai ethical principles without naming them: absolute loyalty to the mission, protection of innocents, acceptance of death over retreat, and respect for enemies.

Why Magikarp Evolves to Gyarados? 🧵

How a 6th-century koi myth became Magikarp's design blueprint

Everyone dunks on Magikarp. Splash. That's it. That's the move. You spend like 20 levels babysitting this useless fish, and the only reason you bother is because you know what's coming.

Which of these words have you caught in anime? Reply 👇

The Dragon Gate legend (龍門, Ryūmon) is a well-documented Chinese and Japanese folk legend, originating in the Shuijing Zhu (6th century CE). It describes koi climbing a waterfall on the Yellow River and transforming into dragons upon reaching the top.
In the Japanese retelling, demons attracted to the koi's glittering scales would raise the height of the waterfall whenever a fish got close to the top.

Magikarp's Japanese name Koikingu (コイキング) directly references koi (鯉, carp). The mechanic - a long grind with a useless Pokémon that transforms into a powerful dragon - mirrors the koi no takinobori legend directly.

鯉の滝登り (koi no takinobori) means the climbing of the waterfall by the carp. It is a Japanese proverb for achieving something against overwhelming odds, composed of koi (carp), no (possessive particle), taki (waterfall), and nobori (climbing).
In traditional versions the transformed dragon is not given a specific name - it is described as a golden dragon ascending to the heavens.

You Already Know How to Count in Japanese 🧵

Hokage titles, Yonko, and Sannin have been teaching you Japanese numbers all along

Every time you called Minato "the Yondaime" you said four. Every time someone referenced the Sannin you said three. Every time you talked about the Yonko era in One Piece you said four again.

Which of these words have you caught in anime? Reply 👇

三代目 (sandaime) means the third-generation holder of the Hokage title. 三 (san) = 3, 代 (dai) = generation or succession, 目 (me) = ordinal suffix that turns a number into nth. The Third Hokage, Hiruzen Sarutobi, holds this title.

三人 (sannin) literally means three people. 三 (san) = 3, 人 (nin) = person or people counter. The legendary Sannin - Jiraiya, Tsunade, and Orochimaru - are simply the three people at the apex of Konoha's shinobi.

四皇 (Yonko) means Four Emperors. 四 (yon) = 4, 皇 (ko) = emperor. The four most powerful pirates who dominate the New World. The number is literally encoded in the title - if you know yon equals 4, the faction name tells you exactly how many there are.
七代目 (nanadaime) means the seventh-generation Hokage. 七 (nana) = 7, 代目 (daime) = nth-generation holder of a title. Naruto Uzumaki is the Nanadaime Hokage, the seventh person to hold the title.
七つ (nanatsu) is the native Japanese reading of 7, from the older counting system (hitotsu, futatsu, mittsu...). 七 (shichi) is the Sino-Japanese reading.

Tamashii (魂) means soul, spirit, or essence - the deepest inner core of a person that persists beyond their physical existence.

Kienai (消えない) means won't disappear, undying, unfading. It combines kieru (消える, to disappear, to go out - used for flames, lights, and presences) with the negative nai (ない). So kienai is the negative of a flame going out: a flame that won't die.

What Do Naruto's Jutsu Names Actually Mean? 🧵

Every technique you've been yelling has a literal translation

Millions of people spent years yelling "RASENGAN" and "CHIDORI" and "KAGE BUNSHIN NO JUTSU" without knowing what any of those words mean. That's not a problem - that's just how anime absorption works. The phonetics come first. The meaning catches up later.
Rasengan (螺旋丸) means Spiraling Sphere. 螺旋 (rasen) means spiral or helix - the character 螺 depicts a spiral shell, and 旋 means to rotate. 丸 (maru) means sphere or round object.

Chidori (千鳥) means One Thousand Birds. Kakashi named the technique after the crackling sound the electrical current makes as it flows through the arm, which sounded to him like a flock of a thousand birds crying out at once.

Sharingan (写輪眼) means Copy Wheel Eye. 写 (sha) is the character for copy or imitate - the same one used in 写真 (shashin, photograph, literally copying truth). 輪 (rin) means wheel or ring, referring to the spinning tomoe pattern.

The Edo in Edo Tensei (穢土転生) uses completely different kanji from the historical city of Edo (江戸). Edo Tensei uses 穢土, meaning defiled earth or impure land - a Buddhist concept for the world of suffering as opposed to the Pure Land of paradise.

Rinnegan (輪廻眼) means Samsara Eye. 輪廻 (rinne) is the Japanese Buddhist term for samsara - the endless cycle of death, rebirth, and suffering. The same concept appears in 輪廻転生 (rinne tensei), the full phrase for reincarnation. 眼 (gan) means eye.

Kage (影) means shadow, silhouette, or the dark shape cast by something. In Japanese the same word covers both a shadow on the ground and the silhouette of a figure. It is also used metaphorically for a trace or vestige of something that was there.

Why Are Uchiha Jutsus Named After Japanese Gods? 🧵

The Shinto myths hiding inside Naruto's eye powers

When Itachi activates Tsukuyomi from his right eye, that is not a coincidence. When Amaterasu erupts from the left, that is not decoration.

Which of these words have you caught in anime? Reply 👇

Amaterasu (天照) is the Shinto goddess of the sun and ruler of the heavens, one of the most important deities in the Kojiki (712 CE). In the original myth, she was born when the god Izanagi washed his left eye after escaping the underworld.
That is exactly how the original myth works. In the Kojiki, when Izanagi washed his left eye, the sun goddess Amaterasu was born. When he washed his right eye, the moon god Tsukuyomi was born.

The Kojiki (古事記, Record of Ancient Matters) is Japan's oldest chronicle, compiled in 712 CE under Emperor Genmei. It records the creation myth, the age of the gods, and the genealogy of the imperial family.
Susanoo (スサノオ) is the Shinto god of storms, born when Izanagi washed his nose during the same purification ritual that produced Amaterasu and Tsukuyomi.
Izanagi (イザナギ) is the male creator deity of Japanese mythology who helped create the islands of Japan with his wife Izanami.

Bushido: The Samurai Code Running Every Anime You Watch 🧵

武士道 explained - the seven virtues behind Tanjiro's compassion, Zoro's loyalty, and Byakuya's honor

You know that moment when Tanjiro bows to a demon he just killed? When Zoro offers his life to Mihawk without hesitation? When Byakuya executes judgment on someone he loves because duty demands it?

Did you already know any of these? Reply 👇
Bushido (武士道, literally 'way of the warrior') is the code of moral conduct followed by the Japanese samurai class.

The seven virtues of Bushido are: Gi (義, righteousness/justice), Yu (勇, courage/bravery), Jin (仁, benevolence/compassion), Rei (礼, respect/etiquette), Makoto (誠, honesty/sincerity), Meiyo (名誉, honor/glory), and Chugi (忠義, loyalty/devotion).

The Hagakure (葉隠), written by samurai Yamamoto Tsunetomo around 1716, contains the most famous quote in samurai philosophy: Bushido to wa shinu koto to mitsuketari (武士道とは死ぬことと見つけたり), meaning 'The way of the samurai is found in death.
Tanjiro Kamado from Demon Slayer embodies the Bushido virtue of Jin (仁, benevolence/compassion), showing mercy even toward the demons he kills.

Zoro's entire character is built on Bushido's virtue of Chugi (忠義, loyalty). His absolute loyalty to Luffy, his oath to become the world's greatest swordsman, and his willingness to die for his captain are all classic Bushido values.

Mama, todoku, and the precise vocabulary for chasing someone who keeps getting further away

Naruto Shippuden had a lot of great openings. But Blue Bird - the third OP by Ikimono-gakari - sits in a different category for most people who grew up watching it.

Which one surprised you most? Drop it below 👇
Blue Bird in Japanese is 青い鳥 (aoi tori). Aoi (青い) means blue or green-blue, a colour that in Japanese traditionally spans sky-blue through spring-green. Tori (鳥) means bird.
Blue Bird is N4 overall - accessible to learners at the beginner-to-intermediate transition. Core vocabulary like jiyuu (freedom), sora (sky), tori (bird), and koe (voice) is N5-N4.
Blue Bird is performed by Ikimonogakari (いきものがかり), a Japanese pop rock band formed in Kanagawa in 1999. The band's name roughly translates to The Animal Keeper or caretaker of living things.

Jiyuu no tori ni nareru (自由の鳥になれる) means I can become a bird of freedom. Jiyuu (自由) means freedom or liberty. No connects it as a modifier to tori (bird). Ni nareru is the potential form of ni naru (to become something) - can become.
Mama (まま) in Japanese grammar means in the unchanged state of / while remaining as. It attaches to a verb (past ta-form) or adjective to express staying in a condition without change.

Learning Japanese with We Are! (One Piece Opening) 🧵

Nakama, jiyuu, and why this is one of the best N5 listening exercises in anime

If you watched One Piece growing up - or even just caught the opening somewhere - you heard We Are! long before you ever thought about studying Japanese.

Which one surprised you most? Drop it below 👇

We Are is an English phrase used as the title of One Piece's first opening. In Japanese the lyrics mix English and Japanese freely. The English We Are functions as a declaration of crew identity - these people are a unit, a crew, a we.

We Are is N4-N5 level overall - one of the most beginner-friendly anime openings from a major series. Core vocabulary (yume for dream, tomodachi/nakama for friend/crewmate, susumu for advance, umi for sea) is N5-N4.

We Are is performed by Hiroshi Kitadani, a Japanese rock vocalist best known as a member of the band ZARD. He recorded We Are in 1999 for the first episode of One Piece and the song remained the opening through episode 47.

Nakama (仲間) is one of the most important words in One Piece and one of the most discussed in anime fandom. It means companion, crewmate, fellow, or person on the same team - but with an emotional weight that varies by context.

Susume (進め) is the bare imperative form of susumu (進む, to advance, to move forward, to make progress). The bare imperative in Japanese, without any politeness suffix, is a direct command. Susume means advance! or move forward! or keep going!

You Already Know 1,000+ Japanese Words 🧵

How English loanwords written in katakana give you a massive head start

Picture this: you're watching Demon Slayer, a character reaches for a drink, and the word that comes out is miruku. You pause. That's... milk. And suddenly you realize - you understood a Japanese word you'd never studied.

Which of these words have you caught in anime? Reply 👇

Katakana is one of Japan's three writing systems and its main job is to write foreign loanwords. When Japanese borrows a word from English, French, German, or any other language, it is usually written in katakana.
Estimates vary, but Japanese has somewhere between 10,000 and 30,000 words borrowed from English.
Miruku (miruku) is the Japanese loanword for milk, borrowed directly from English and written in katakana as miruku. You will see it on milk cartons, in cafe menus, and in recipes across Japan.
Katakana has 46 base characters and most learners can recognize all of them within a few days of focused practice. The characters look more angular than hiragana, which makes them visually distinct.

Hiragana and katakana both represent the same 46 sounds in Japanese but use different character shapes. Hiragana is rounder and cursive-looking - it is used for native Japanese words and grammatical particles.

Rurouni Kenshin's Japan Was Real 🧵

The samurai who lost everything when the Meiji era began

If you've watched Rurouni Kenshin, you know Kenshin is a wanderer in a Japan that feels like it's moving on without him. Everyone around him is cutting their topknots, wearing Western clothes, building telegraph lines.

Did you already know any of these? Reply 👇
Rurouni Kenshin is set in Meiji 11, which is 1878. This is exactly one year after the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877 ended - the last major armed uprising of samurai against the Meiji government.

After 1868, samurai lost their hereditary stipends (abolished by 1876), were forbidden from carrying swords in public by the Haitōrei edict of 1876, and were reclassified as shizoku (warrior families) with no special privileges.
Saigo Takamori, the leader of the Satsuma Rebellion and widely called the last true samurai, is a key historical figure behind the manga's themes.

Saito Hajime was a real historical figure who served as a captain in the Shinsengumi, the elite pro-shogunate sword force. After the Meiji Restoration he reinvented himself as a police officer - exactly as depicted in Rurouni Kenshin. He lived until 1915.
The Haitōrei edict (廃刀令) was a law passed in March 1876 that prohibited anyone except military personnel and police officers from wearing swords in public.
